rows.stem: The ratio of potential difference across AB in the circuit shown for the case (i) when switch S is closed and (ii) when S is open is :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — the stem says only 'the circuit shown'; the resistor values and the branch the switch sits in exist nowhere but the drawing. What is drawn: a single loop containing a cell labelled V along the bottom. Three labelled nodes lie on the upper path — A on the left, B in the middle, C on the right. A single resistor lies between A and B. Between B and C the path splits into two parallel branches, drawn as a lens shape; the upper branch carries one resistor and, to its right, a switch labelled S drawn as an open blade; the lower branch carries two resistors in series. WITHHELD: every resistance value, since the ratio asked for follows directly from them. Page idx 4.
rows.solution:
**The answer is (D): 2.**

**Read the circuit.** A \(2R\) runs from \(A\) to \(B\); between \(B\) and \(C\) there are two parallel branches — an upper one of \(3R\) in series with the switch \(S\), and a lower one of \(4R\) and \(2R\) in series (that is, \(6R\)); and \(C\) returns to the battery \(V\).

**The potential difference "across AB" is the drop across that \(2R\)**, so in each case it is simply \(I \times 2R\) with \(I\) the current the battery drives.

**Case (i): switch CLOSED.**

Both branches carry current, so between \(B\) and \(C\):

\(R_{BC} = \dfrac{3R \times 6R}{3R + 6R} = \dfrac{18R^{2}}{9R} = 2R\)

Total circuit resistance \(= 2R + 2R = 4R\), so

\(I_{\text{closed}} = \dfrac{V}{4R} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad V_{AB} = \dfrac{V}{4R}\times 2R = \dfrac{V}{2}\)

**Case (ii): switch OPEN.**

The upper branch is broken, so **only the \(6R\) path survives**:

Total resistance \(= 2R + 6R = 8R\), so

\(I_{\text{open}} = \dfrac{V}{8R} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad V_{AB} = \dfrac{V}{8R}\times 2R = \dfrac{V}{4}\)

**The ratio.**

\(\dfrac{V_{AB}\left(\text{closed}\right)}{V_{AB}\left(\text{open}\right)} = \dfrac{V/2}{V/4}\)

\(\boxed{\ = 2\ }\)

**A shortcut that skips the voltages entirely.** \(V_{AB} = 2RI\) in both cases, so the ratio of the potential differences is just the ratio of the **currents**, which is the inverse ratio of the total resistances:

\(\dfrac{I_{\text{closed}}}{I_{\text{open}}} = \dfrac{8R}{4R} = 2\)

**Why closing the switch RAISES the drop across AB.** Adding the second branch in parallel **lowers** the resistance between \(B\) and \(C\), so the battery drives more current round the whole circuit — and more current through the \(2R\) means a larger drop across it. The \(2R\) and the \(B\)-\(C\) network are in **series**, so they share the emf: whatever the network loses, \(AB\) gains.

**The distractors, and where they come from.** Option (A), \(\tfrac{1}{4}\), and (B), \(\tfrac{1}{2}\), are the ratio taken the wrong way round or the resistances not combined. Option (C), \(1\), would mean the switch changes nothing — true only if the upper branch had infinite resistance, which is exactly what "open" makes it, so it is the answer for the other case.

**A check on the extreme.** If the upper branch were a plain wire (zero resistance), closing \(S\) would short out \(B\)-\(C\) entirely, leaving \(2R\) alone; the current would be \(V/2R\) and \(V_{AB} = V\) — four times the open-switch value. The actual \(3R\) gives a more modest doubling.

rows.stem: A particle of mass m and charge q moving with velocity \(v\,\hat{i}\) is subjected to a uniform electric field \(E\,\hat{j}\). The particle will initially have a tendency to move in a circle of radius :
rows.solution:
**The answer is (C): \(\dfrac{mv^{2}}{qE}\) in the x-y plane.**

**The situation.** The velocity is \(v\hat{i}\) and the force is \(qE\hat{j}\) — a **constant** force, **perpendicular** to the initial velocity.

**Why a circle at all, and only "initially".** A constant force perpendicular to the velocity is, at that instant, exactly a centripetal force, so the path has a definite **radius of curvature** there. But the force stays fixed in direction while the velocity turns, so the two stop being perpendicular immediately — and the real path is a **parabola**, not a circle. The question asks for the circle the motion "initially has a tendency" to follow, which is the **circle of curvature** at \(t = 0\).

**The radius.** Equating the applied force to the centripetal requirement at that instant:

\(\dfrac{mv^{2}}{r} = qE\)

\(\boxed{\ r = \dfrac{mv^{2}}{qE}\ }\)

**The plane.** The velocity lies along \(x\) and the force along \(y\), so the motion is confined to the **x-y plane** — there is nothing at all along \(z\). That alone eliminates options (B) and (D), which name the wrong planes.

**Option (A) is the MAGNETIC answer, and that is the whole trap.** For a charge in a magnetic field, \(qvB = mv^{2}/r\) gives

\(r = \dfrac{mv}{qB}\)

with a **single** power of \(v\), because the magnetic force itself contains a factor of \(v\). In an **electric** field the force \(qE\) does **not** depend on speed, so nothing cancels and \(v^{2}\) survives. The two formulas differ by exactly one power of \(v\), and option (A) is the magnetic one with \(B\) rewritten as \(E\).

**A dimensional check settles it without any physics.** \(qE\) is a force, so \(mv^{2}/qE\) has dimensions of (mass × velocity²)/force = energy/force = **length** \(\checkmark\). Meanwhile \(mv/qE\) gives momentum/force = **time**, not a length — so option (A) is dimensionally wrong here, however familiar it looks. Options (B) and (D) carry \(E^{2}\) and are wrong on dimensions too.

**The contrast worth keeping.**

| | Electric field | Magnetic field |
|---|---|---|
| Force | \(qE\), independent of \(v\) | \(qvB\), proportional to \(v\) |
| Radius of curvature | \(\dfrac{mv^{2}}{qE}\) | \(\dfrac{mv}{qB}\) |
| Actual path | **parabola** | **circle** (or helix) |
| Work done | non-zero — speed changes | **zero** — speed constant |

The magnetic case gives a genuine circle precisely because the force keeps turning with the velocity; the electric one does not, which is why the question has to say "initially".

rows.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
rows.stem: The wavelength of a photon is equal to the wavelength associated with an electron. Both will have the same value of :
rows.solution:
**The answer is (D): linear momentum.**

**The one relation that covers both.**

For a **photon**: \(p = \dfrac{h}{\lambda}\), from \(E = pc\) and \(E = hc/\lambda\).

For an **electron**: \(p = \dfrac{h}{\lambda}\), by de Broglie's hypothesis.

**The same equation holds for both**, so equal wavelengths force equal momenta:

\(\boxed{\ p_{\text{photon}} = p_{\text{electron}} = \dfrac{h}{\lambda}\ }\)

**That \(\lambda = h/p\) applies to both is exactly de Broglie's point** — he took a relation established for light and asserted it for matter. The question is really asking whether that unification is understood.

**Why the other three differ.**

**Energy.** The two depend on momentum quite differently:

\(E_{\text{photon}} = pc \qquad\text{against}\qquad E_{\text{electron}} = \dfrac{p^{2}}{2m}\)

The photon's energy is **linear** in \(p\), the electron's **quadratic**. At \(\lambda = 1\ \mathring{\mathrm{A}}\), for instance, the photon carries about \(12\ 400\) eV while the electron carries about \(150\) eV — a factor of \(80\).

**Velocity.** The photon travels at \(c\); the electron, having mass, cannot. For the \(1\ \mathring{\mathrm{A}}\) case the electron moves at roughly \(7 \times 10^{6}\) m/s, some \(2\%\) of \(c\).

**Angular momentum.** Not determined by wavelength at all — it depends on the state of motion about some axis, and the question fixes nothing about that. A photon carries intrinsic spin angular momentum \(\hbar\); an electron's is \(\hbar/2\).

**The general lesson.** Wavelength and momentum are two names for the same physical quantity, tied by the universal constant \(h\) — so **matching one always matches the other**, for any particle whatever, massive or not. Energy and velocity, by contrast, require the particle's mass to compute, and mass is precisely what a photon and an electron do not share.

**A memory hook.** \(p = h/\lambda\) has **no mass in it**. Any quantity whose formula needs \(m\) cannot be shared between a photon and an electron on wavelength alone; any quantity whose formula does not, is shared.

rows.stem:
(a) What is the difference between 'velocity' and 'drift velocity' of electrons in a current-carrying conductor.
(b) A copper wire of uniform cross-sectional area carries a current of \(3{\cdot}4\) A. The drift velocity of conduction electrons is \(0{\cdot}2\) mm/s. If the number density of electrons in copper is \(8{\cdot}5 \times 10^{28}\) m\(^{-3}\), find the area of cross-section of the wire.
rows.solution:
**(a) Velocity against drift velocity.**

| | **Velocity** (thermal / instantaneous) | **Drift velocity** |
|---|---|---|
| What it is | the actual velocity of an individual electron, its rate of change of displacement | the **average** velocity of all the free electrons under the applied field |
| Cause | random **thermal** motion; present even with no field | the applied **electric field** |
| Magnitude | large, about \(10^{5}\) m/s at room temperature | very small, about \(10^{-4}\) m/s |
| Direction | completely **random** | **opposite** to \(\vec{E}\) (the electron's charge is negative) |
| Average over all electrons | **ZERO** | \(v_d = \dfrac{eE\tau}{m}\), non-zero |
| Carries current? | **No** | **Yes** |

**The relationship between them.** The drift is not a separate motion but a tiny systematic **bias** superimposed on the violent random one. The thermal speeds are some \(10^{9}\) times larger, yet they average to nothing because they point every way equally; only the minute drift survives the averaging, and that is what constitutes the current.

**(b) The cross-sectional area.**

\(I = neAv_d \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad A = \dfrac{I}{nev_d}\)

**Substituting**, with \(v_d = 0{\cdot}2\ \mathrm{mm/s} = 0{\cdot}2 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m/s}\):

\(A = \dfrac{3{\cdot}4}{\left(8{\cdot}5 \times 10^{28}\right)\left(1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-19}\right)\left(0{\cdot}2 \times 10^{-3}\right)}\)

**Taking the denominator in stages:**

\(\left(8{\cdot}5 \times 10^{28}\right)\left(1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-19}\right) = 1{\cdot}36 \times 10^{10}\)

\(\left(1{\cdot}36 \times 10^{10}\right)\left(2 \times 10^{-4}\right) = 2{\cdot}72 \times 10^{6}\)

\(A = \dfrac{3{\cdot}4}{2{\cdot}72 \times 10^{6}}\)

\(\boxed{\ A = 1{\cdot}25 \times 10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m^{2}} = 1{\cdot}25\ \mathrm{mm^{2}}\ }\)

**The millimetre-per-second conversion is the only hazard** — reading \(0{\cdot}2\) mm/s as \(0{\cdot}2\) m/s gives an area a thousand times too small.

**A sense of the answer.** \(1{\cdot}25\ \mathrm{mm^{2}}\) corresponds to a wire about \(1{\cdot}3\) mm across — ordinary domestic wiring, and entirely plausible for \(3{\cdot}4\) A.

**What the drift speed tells us.** At \(0{\cdot}2\) mm/s an electron takes nearly **an hour and a half** to travel a single metre of this wire. Yet the current begins everywhere the instant the circuit closes, because the **electric field** propagates at nearly the speed of light and sets every electron in the wire drifting at once. Nothing has to make the journey.

rows.stem: An alpha particle and a deuterium ion are accelerated through the same potential difference. These are then directed towards a target nucleus to make head-on collision. It is observed that their distance of closest approach is the same. Justify it theoretically.
rows.solution:
**What has to be shown.** That two projectiles of different charge and different mass, accelerated through the **same** potential difference, reach the **same** distance of closest approach to a given nucleus.

**Step 1 — the kinetic energy on arrival.** A particle of charge \(q\) accelerated from rest through a potential difference \(V\) gains

\(K = qV\)

So the alpha particle \(\left(q = 2e\right)\) arrives with \(2eV\), and the deuteron \(\left(q = e\right)\) with only \(eV\) — the alpha has **twice** the energy.

**Step 2 — the condition at closest approach.** The particle stops momentarily, so all its kinetic energy has become electrostatic potential energy against the target nucleus of charge \(Ze\):

\(K = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot\dfrac{\left(Ze\right)q}{d}\)

**Step 3 — substitute and watch \(q\) cancel.** Putting \(K = qV\):

\(qV = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot\dfrac{Zeq}{d}\)

**The projectile's charge \(q\) appears on BOTH sides and divides out:**

\(V = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot\dfrac{Ze}{d}\)

\(\boxed{\ d = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot\dfrac{Ze}{V}\ }\)

**The result depends only on the target's charge \(Z\) and the accelerating voltage \(V\)** — nothing about the projectile survives. Since both particles were accelerated through the same \(V\) towards the same nucleus, both must stop at the same \(d\). That is the justification.

**Why the cancellation happens, in words.** A doubly charged projectile gains **twice** the energy from the same potential difference, but it is also repelled **twice** as strongly by the target. The extra energy is exactly consumed by the extra repulsion, and the turning point is unmoved.

**Note that the MASS never entered at all.** The alpha is about twice the deuteron's mass, so it arrives moving more slowly — but the calculation is an **energy** balance from start to finish, and speed is never needed. Mass would matter if the question asked how long the journey took, or what the momentum was, but not for where it stops.

**A numerical illustration.** For a gold target \(\left(Z = 79\right)\) and \(V = 4 \times 10^{6}\) volts:

\(d = \dfrac{9 \times 10^{9} \times 79 \times 1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-19}}{4 \times 10^{6}} \approx 2{\cdot}8 \times 10^{-14}\ \mathrm{m}\)

the same for both, and comfortably outside the nucleus — which is why Rutherford's purely Coulomb analysis holds.

**The practical corollary.** In a scattering experiment the closest approach is controlled entirely by the **accelerating voltage**, not by the choice of projectile. To probe deeper one must raise the voltage; switching to a more highly charged ion achieves nothing.

rows.stem: A tank is filled with a liquid of refractive index \(\sqrt{2}\), up to a height of 30 cm. A tiny bulb is glowing at the bottom of the tank. Calculate the diameter of an opaque disc floating symmetrically on the liquid surface that can cut off completely the light from the bulb that comes out of the liquid surface.
rows.solution:
**The physical picture.** Light leaves the bulb in all directions, but only rays striking the surface at **less than the critical angle** can emerge. Everything steeper is totally internally reflected back into the liquid. So the light escapes through a **circle** on the surface, directly above the bulb — the base of a cone of half-angle \(i_c\) with its apex at the bulb.

**A disc that covers exactly that circle cuts off all the emerging light.**

**Step 1 — the critical angle.**

\(\sin i_c = \dfrac{1}{n} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad i_c = 45^\circ\)

**Step 2 — the radius of the circle.** The cone has apex at the bulb, height \(d = 30\) cm and half-angle \(i_c\), so its base radius is

\(r = d\tan i_c = 30 \times \tan 45^\circ = 30 \times 1 = 30\ \mathrm{cm}\)

**Step 3 — the diameter.**

\(\boxed{\ D = 2r = 60\ \mathrm{cm}\ }\)

**The \(\sqrt{2}\) is chosen to make \(\tan i_c = 1\) exactly**, so the radius simply equals the depth. That is worth spotting: for a liquid of index \(\sqrt{2}\) the escape circle is always as wide as the tank is deep.

**The general formula**, for any index:

\(\tan i_c = \dfrac{\sin i_c}{\cos i_c} = \dfrac{1/n}{\sqrt{1 - 1/n^{2}}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{n^{2} - 1}}\)

\(D = \dfrac{2d}{\sqrt{n^{2} - 1}}\)

which gives \(2 \times 30/\sqrt{2 - 1} = 60\) cm here \(\checkmark\). The \(n\) cancels out of \(\tan i_c\) entirely, which is why \(n^{2} - 1\) appears rather than a lone \(n\).

**Reading the dependence.** A **denser** liquid gives a smaller critical angle and so a **smaller** escape window — the disc needed would be narrower. As \(n \to 1\) the liquid becomes optically like air, there is no total internal reflection at all, and the required disc becomes infinite: the formula correctly diverges.

**The distinction between RADIUS and DIAMETER** is where marks are most often lost here. The cone's geometry gives the radius; the question asks for the diameter of the disc, which is twice it.

**Where this is seen.** It is why a coin at the bottom of a pool is visible only through a limited patch of surface, and why a fish looking upward sees the entire world above the water compressed into a circular window — **Snell's window** — of half-angle \(49^\circ\) for water. Outside that circle the surface looks like a mirror, reflecting the pool bottom back.

rows.stem:
(a) Differentiate between 'nuclear fission' and 'nuclear fusion'. Briefly discuss one example of each.
(b) Draw a graph of potential energy between a pair of nucleons as a function of their separation.
rows.solution:
**(a) Nuclear fission against nuclear fusion.**

| | **Nuclear fission** | **Nuclear fusion** |
|---|---|---|
| Process | a **heavy** nucleus **splits** into two lighter ones of comparable mass | two **light** nuclei **combine** into a heavier one |
| Typical fuel | \({}^{235}\)U, \({}^{239}\)Pu | \({}^{2}\)H, \({}^{3}\)H, \({}^{1}\)H |
| How it is started | capture of a **slow neutron** — no barrier, since the neutron is uncharged | enormous **temperature**, \(\sim 10^{7}\) K or more, to overcome Coulomb repulsion |
| Energy per reaction | about **200 MeV** | about **3 to 20 MeV** |
| Energy per **nucleon** | about \(0{\cdot}85\) MeV | about \(3{\cdot}5\) MeV — **greater** |
| Chain reaction? | **Yes**, via the neutrons released | No; it is sustained by temperature |
| Products | radioactive fission fragments | usually stable, little radioactive waste |

**One example of fission.**

\({}^{235}_{92}\mathrm{U} + {}^{1}_{0}\mathrm{n} \longrightarrow {}^{141}_{56}\mathrm{Ba} + {}^{92}_{36}\mathrm{Kr} + 3\,{}^{1}_{0}\mathrm{n} + \sim 200\ \mathrm{MeV}\)

A slow neutron is absorbed, the nucleus becomes unstable and splits. **The three neutrons released can each induce further fissions**, so a **chain reaction** is possible — controlled by moderators and control rods in a reactor, uncontrolled in a weapon. Most of the energy appears as kinetic energy of the two fragments.

**One example of fusion.**

\({}^{2}_{1}\mathrm{H} + {}^{2}_{1}\mathrm{H} \longrightarrow {}^{3}_{2}\mathrm{He} + {}^{1}_{0}\mathrm{n} + 3{\cdot}27\ \mathrm{MeV}\)

Two deuterons must approach within about \(1\) fm, which means overcoming their mutual electrostatic repulsion — hence the enormous temperatures. **This is how the Sun shines**, through the proton-proton chain that converts four hydrogen nuclei into helium with a release of \(26{\cdot}7\) MeV.

**Why BOTH release energy.** The binding energy per nucleon curve **peaks near iron** \(\left(A \approx 56\right)\) at about \(8{\cdot}8\) MeV. Heavy nuclei move towards the peak by splitting; light nuclei move towards it by joining. Any reaction that carries nucleons closer to iron releases energy, and that single curve explains both processes at once.

**(b) Potential energy of a pair of nucleons against their separation.**

*To draw it:* potential energy \(U\) on the vertical axis, separation \(r\) on the horizontal, with \(r\) in femtometres.

**The three features that must appear:**

**A steep POSITIVE branch for \(r < 0{\cdot}8\) fm.** At very small separations the force is strongly **repulsive** — the "hard core" — and \(U\) rises sharply. This is what stops nucleons collapsing into one another and gives nuclei a roughly constant density.

**A zero crossing at \(r_0 \approx 0{\cdot}8\) fm**, where the force changes from repulsive to attractive.

**A deep NEGATIVE minimum of about \(-100\) MeV near \(r \approx 1\) fm**, the equilibrium separation at which nucleons sit.

**Then a rapid rise back towards zero**, the curve flattening onto the axis by about \(3\) fm.

**What the shape encodes.** The **short range** is the flattening beyond a few fm — beyond that, nucleons simply do not feel one another, which is why the nuclear force **saturates** and the binding energy per nucleon stays roughly constant instead of growing with \(A\). The **depth** of about \(100\) MeV is what makes the force strong enough to overcome the Coulomb repulsion between protons, which is only a few MeV at these separations.

**And the curve is the same for every pair.** Proton-proton, neutron-neutron and proton-neutron all follow it — the nuclear force is **charge-independent**. (For two protons the Coulomb repulsion is superimposed on top, but it is a small correction at \(1\) fm.)

rows.stem:
(a) A concave mirror has radius of curvature 20 cm. Calculate the distance of an object from the mirror so as to form an image of magnification – 2. Also find the location of the image.
(b) If the silver coating around the centre of a concave mirror is removed, will the mirror still form the image of an object ? Justify your answer.
rows.solution:
**(a) Object and image distances.**

**The data, with signs.** For a **concave** mirror the centre of curvature and the focus lie in front of the mirror, so

\(R = -20\ \mathrm{cm} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad f = \dfrac{R}{2} = -10\ \mathrm{cm}\)

**Translate the magnification.**

\(m = -\dfrac{v}{u} = -2 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad v = 2u\)

**\(m\) is NEGATIVE, so the image is real and inverted** — and it is that sign, not the size, that fixes the geometry. A magnification of \(+2\) would describe a virtual erect image and give a quite different object position.

**Apply the mirror formula.**

\(\dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}\)

\(\dfrac{1}{2u} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{-10}\)

\(\dfrac{1 + 2}{2u} = -\dfrac{1}{10} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \dfrac{3}{2u} = -\dfrac{1}{10}\)

\(2u = -30 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \boxed{\ u = -15\ \mathrm{cm}\ }\)

and then

\(\boxed{\ v = 2u = -30\ \mathrm{cm}\ }\)

**Reading the signs.** Both are negative, so **both the object and the image are in FRONT of the mirror** — the object \(15\) cm away, the image \(30\) cm away. The image is **real** (it could be caught on a screen), **inverted**, and twice the size.

**A check against the mirror's known behaviour.** With \(f = 10\) cm and \(R = 20\) cm, the object at \(15\) cm lies **between \(F\) and \(C\)** — and the standard result for that position is an image **beyond \(C\)**, real, inverted and magnified. The image at \(30\) cm is indeed beyond \(C\) at \(20\) cm. \(\checkmark\)

**And a check on the magnification:** \(m = -v/u = -\left(-30\right)/\left(-15\right) = -2\ \checkmark\)

**(b) Removing the silver coating from the centre.**

\(\boxed{\ \text{YES — the mirror still forms the COMPLETE image, but it is FAINTER.}\ }\)

**Why the image is complete and not partial.** **Every point of the mirror surface receives light from every point of the object.** Rays leave each object point in all directions, strike the whole mirror, and are brought together at the corresponding image point. So the outer annulus that remains silvered still receives rays from **every** part of the object, and still converges each bundle to its proper image point. The laws of reflection are unaffected for whatever surface survives.

**What does change is the INTENSITY.** Removing the central patch reduces the **area** collecting light, so fewer rays reach each image point and the image is correspondingly dimmer. The whole picture fades; no part of it disappears.

**The common misconception this tests.** Students often expect the middle of the image to vanish — as though each part of the mirror made its own part of the image. That would be true of a **projected shadow**, but not of an image: a mirror or lens is not a one-to-one map of surface onto picture.

**The same principle in familiar form.** Cover half a camera lens or half a telescope's aperture and the image stays whole, merely dimmer. It is also why a broken mirror fragment still shows a complete reflection, and why the central obstruction of a reflecting telescope's secondary mirror costs brightness rather than picture.

rows.stem: State Kirchhoff's laws. Apply these laws to find the values of current flowing in the three branches of the given circuit.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — the stem says only 'the given circuit'; every cell emf and every resistance exists nowhere but the drawing. Read on this paper's own page: a rectangular outline whose left and right sides are plain conductors joining three horizontal branches. The topmost branch carries a cell labelled 5 V and, to its right, a resistor labelled 2 ohm. A middle horizontal branch bridges the two sides and carries a cell labelled 10 V and, to its right, a resistor labelled 1 ohm. The bottom branch carries a single resistor labelled 2 ohm and no cell. WITHHELD: the orientation of the long and short plates of the two cells, i.e. their relative polarity, which is what fixes the signs of the three currents the question asks for. Page idx 16.
rows.solution:
**Kirchhoff's laws.**

**Junction rule (first law).** At any junction in a circuit, the **algebraic sum of the currents is zero** — the total current entering equals the total leaving:

\(\sum I = 0\)

This expresses **conservation of charge**: charge cannot accumulate at a point in a steady current.

**Loop rule (second law).** Around any **closed loop**, the algebraic sum of the changes in potential is zero:

\(\sum \Delta V = 0\)

This expresses **conservation of energy**: a charge carried once round a loop returns to the same potential, so the emfs supplied must equal the drops across the resistances.

**Applying them to the network.** Three branches connect the same two rails — the left rail and the right rail:

*Top branch:* a \(5\) V cell (positive terminal on the **right**) in series with \(2\ \Omega\).

*Middle branch:* a \(10\) V cell (positive terminal on the **left**) in series with \(1\ \Omega\).

*Bottom branch:* a plain \(2\ \Omega\).

**The two cells OPPOSE each other**, which is what makes the arithmetic interesting.

**Solving by node potentials**, which is the shortest route when every branch joins the same two nodes. Let

\(U = V_{\text{left}} - V_{\text{right}}\)

and let each branch current be counted positive when it flows **left to right**.

*Top:* tracing left to right we cross the cell from \(-\) to \(+\) (a rise of \(5\)), then drop \(2I_1\):

\(U + 5 - 2I_1 = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad I_1 = \dfrac{U + 5}{2}\)

*Middle:* we cross from \(+\) to \(-\) (a fall of \(10\)), then drop \(1 \times I_2\):

\(U - 10 - I_2 = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad I_2 = U - 10\)

*Bottom:*

\(U - 2I_3 = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad I_3 = \dfrac{U}{2}\)

**Junction rule at the left rail** — all three branches leave it, so their currents must sum to zero:

\(\dfrac{U + 5}{2} + \left(U - 10\right) + \dfrac{U}{2} = 0\)

Multiplying by \(2\):

\(U + 5 + 2U - 20 + U = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 4U = 15 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad U = 3{\cdot}75\ \mathrm{V}\)

**The three currents.**

\(\boxed{\ I_1 = \dfrac{3{\cdot}75 + 5}{2} = 4{\cdot}375\ \mathrm{A} = \dfrac{35}{8}\ \mathrm{A}, \ \text{left to right through the 5 V branch}\ }\)

\(\boxed{\ I_2 = 3{\cdot}75 - 10 = -6{\cdot}25\ \mathrm{A}, \ \text{i.e. } \dfrac{25}{4}\ \mathrm{A} \ \text{RIGHT to LEFT through the 10 V branch}\ }\)

\(\boxed{\ I_3 = \dfrac{3{\cdot}75}{2} = 1{\cdot}875\ \mathrm{A} = \dfrac{15}{8}\ \mathrm{A}, \ \text{left to right through the } 2\ \Omega\ }\)

**Check by the junction rule**, using the equation not used to find them: \(6{\cdot}25\) A arrives at the left rail from the middle branch, and \(4{\cdot}375 + 1{\cdot}875 = 6{\cdot}25\) A leaves through the other two. \(\checkmark\)

**Reading the result.** The \(10\) V cell dominates: it drives current out of its positive terminal into the left rail, and that current divides between the top and bottom branches on the way back. In the top branch it flows **backwards** through the \(5\) V cell, which is therefore being **charged** rather than discharged.

**A caution about the printed scheme's third line.** It gives \(I_1 = -\tfrac{35}{8}\) and \(I_2 = +\tfrac{25}{4}\), and then states \(I_1 + I_2 = -\tfrac{15}{8}\) A. But those two values sum to \(-\tfrac{35}{8} + \tfrac{50}{8} = +\tfrac{15}{8}\), so the minus sign there does not follow from its own working. The magnitude, \(\tfrac{15}{8} = 1{\cdot}875\) A, is correct — and the direction is settled independently by the potentials: the left rail sits \(3{\cdot}75\) V **above** the right, so current in the plain \(2\ \Omega\) must flow from left to right.

**Why the numbers are awkward.** An unbalanced network with two **opposing** cells of unequal emf has no reason to give round currents. Eighths are the honest answer here; \(4{\cdot}375\) A is exact, and rounding it away loses the check above.

rows.subtopic: Bohr Model of the Hydrogen Atom
rows.stem:
In Bohr model of hydrogen atom, an electron is revolving in second orbit. Find the value of :
(i) angular momentum of electron,
(ii) radius of the orbit, and
(iii) kinetic energy of electron.
Take radius of first orbit of hydrogen atom as \(0{\cdot}5\) \(\mathring{\mathrm{A}}\).
rows.solution:
**(i) The angular momentum.**

Bohr's quantisation condition:

\(L = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}\)

For \(n = 2\):

\(L = \dfrac{2 \times 6{\cdot}63 \times 10^{-34}}{2\pi} = \dfrac{6{\cdot}63 \times 10^{-34}}{3{\cdot}14}\)

\(\boxed{\ L = 2{\cdot}11 \times 10^{-34}\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{2}\,s^{-1}}\ }\)

**The two \(2\)s cancel**, leaving simply \(h/\pi\) — worth noticing, since it removes a step. In terms of \(\hbar = h/2\pi = 1{\cdot}055 \times 10^{-34}\) J s, this orbit carries exactly \(2\hbar\).

**(ii) The radius.**

\(r_n = n^{2}r_1\)

\(r_2 = 4 \times 0{\cdot}5\ \mathring{\mathrm{A}}\)

\(\boxed{\ r_2 = 2{\cdot}0\ \mathring{\mathrm{A}} = 2{\cdot}0 \times 10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m}\ }\)

**The radius goes as \(n^{2}\)**, not as \(n\), so the second orbit is **four** times the first — not twice. That square is the commonest slip in this part.

**(iii) The kinetic energy.**

**The total energy first:**

\(E_n = -\dfrac{13{\cdot}6}{n^{2}}\ \mathrm{eV} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad E_2 = -\dfrac{13{\cdot}6}{4} = -3{\cdot}4\ \mathrm{eV}\)

**Then the kinetic energy**, using the relation that holds for any inverse-square attraction:

\(K = -E\)

\(\boxed{\ K = +3{\cdot}4\ \mathrm{eV} = 5{\cdot}44 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}\ }\)

**Why \(K = -E\), since it looks like a trick.** Balancing the Coulomb attraction against the centripetal requirement gives

\(\dfrac{mv^{2}}{r} = \dfrac{ke^{2}}{r^{2}} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad K = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^{2} = \dfrac{ke^{2}}{2r}\)

while the potential energy is \(U = -ke^{2}/r = -2K\). So

\(E = K + U = K - 2K = -K\)

**The kinetic energy is always the positive of the total, and the potential energy twice the total** — the virial relation for a \(1/r\) force, and it holds for planetary orbits just as for this one.

**The three signs worth keeping straight at \(n = 2\):**

\(K = +3{\cdot}4\ \mathrm{eV}, \qquad U = -6{\cdot}8\ \mathrm{eV}, \qquad E = -3{\cdot}4\ \mathrm{eV}\)

**The energy is NEGATIVE because the electron is bound** — \(3{\cdot}4\) eV would have to be supplied to remove it to infinity from this orbit. The kinetic energy, being a real motion, is of course positive.

**A note on the given \(r_1\).** The question says to take \(0{\cdot}5\ \mathring{\mathrm{A}}\); the accepted Bohr radius is \(0{\cdot}529\ \mathring{\mathrm{A}}\). Using the rounded value keeps the arithmetic clean and changes \(r_2\) from \(2{\cdot}12\) to \(2{\cdot}00\ \mathring{\mathrm{A}}\) — a difference of about \(6\%\), and worth knowing about rather than mistaking the rounded figure for the true constant.
